docs.title: What is paulrun?
docs.text:
paulrun runs hand-written markdown runbooks.

A runbook is a normal markdown file that a person can read and follow without paulrun. Mark a code block run, and paulrun runs it for you. Everything else stays documentation.

docs.title: Example runbook
docs.text:
---
title: Release my-package
output_path: logs/release-<VERSION>.md
inputs:
  - name: VERSION
    description: The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0
    pattern: '^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$'
---

# Releasing my-package

## Run the tests

```sh run
make test
```

## Tag the release

```sh run
git tag <VERSION>
git push origin <VERSION>
```

## Publish on GitHub

```confirm
Create a GitHub release from tag <VERSION>.
```

Check it, then run it:

paulrun check RELEASING.md
paulrun RELEASING.md

paulrun asks for the version, shows you the plan, and runs each step in order, streaming every command's output as it goes. It stops at the first command that fails, and waits for you at the GitHub step, since that one is done by hand:

VERSION (The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0): 1.2.0
Release my-package
directory: /home/you/Projects/my-package
inputs: VERSION=1.2.0
  1. Run the tests
  2. Tag the release
  3. Publish on GitHub
2 run blocks
Start? [y/N] y

=== Run the tests ===
    make test
...
exit 0 (4.2s)

=== Tag the release ===
    git tag 1.2.0
    git push origin 1.2.0
...
exit 0 (1.3s)

=== Publish on GitHub ===
Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0.
Continue? [y/N] y

finished: ok (12.8s)
transcript: logs/release-1.2.0.md

Every run is also recorded in logs/release-1.2.0.md, so you can see afterwards exactly what ran and what it printed.

docs.title: Your runbook library
docs.text:
Keep runbooks you use across projects in ~/runbooks, and run them by name from anywhere:

$ paulrun library
library: /home/you/runbooks
rebuild-frontend     Rebuild the frontend
update-project-deps  Update a project's dependencies

$ cd ~/Projects/website
$ paulrun rebuild-frontend

A book runs in the folder you're in, so one book works for every project. See Your runbook library.

docs.title: Why use paulrun?
docs.text:
Release steps get forgotten. Writing them down helps; making the written-down version run itself fixes it.

  • It's just markdown - A runbook reads like documentation, renders on GitHub, and works fine without paulrun.
  • Check before you run - paulrun check finds broken frontmatter, undeclared placeholders and syntax errors.
  • See what would happen - paulrun --dry RELEASING.md shows every command with its inputs filled in, and runs nothing.
  • Inputs and secrets - Ask for values once, check them against a pattern, and keep secrets off the screen and out of the log.
  • Manual steps too - confirm blocks pause for the things only a person can do.
  • A record of every run - An optional transcript keeps every command, its output and how it finished.
  • More than shell - Shell and Python blocks are built in, and other languages can be added as backends.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Install paulrun
  • The runbook format: everything a runbook can contain
  • The command line: every command, flag and exit code
  • Your runbook library: runbooks you keep for yourself, and run from anywhere
  • Backends: the languages paulrun runs, and adding your own

• A runbook can set step: true in its frontmatter to always run as if --step was given, asking before each run block. --no-step runs it straight through. check reports a step that isn't true or false.
  • The book picker, paulrun run with no runbook, now takes q to quit, and says so: Run which? (q to quit).
  • A block skipped under --step is now shown, and recorded in the transcript, as skipped rather than skipped (--step), since step: true skips blocks too.

docs.title: A runbook library
docs.text:
• keep runbooks you use across projects in ~/runbooks, or wherever PAULRUN_LIBRARY says. Then run one by name from anywhere, e.g. paulrun rebuild-frontend. run, check and inputs all take a book's name as well as a path, and a file where you are is always used before a book with the same name. paulrun library lists the books in your library, with each one's title and description. paulrun run, with no runbook, lists them by number and runs the one you pick.

  • A new docs page, Your runbook library, with a worked example of a book that rebuilds a frontend under nvm.

  • Breaking: paulrun go is now paulrun run, and you don't need to type it: paulrun RELEASING.md runs RELEASING.md. Anything after paulrun that isn't a command is a runbook to run, so paulrun go is no longer a command. paulrun on its own still shows help.

  • Breaking: blocks now run in the folder you run paulrun from, not the folder the runbook is in. A relative output_path is now relative to that folder too. A runbook kept at the root of its project, run from there, works as before. One run as paulrun path/to/RUNBOOK.md from another folder now works on that other folder and writes its transcript there. This includes blocks run by external backends, whose cwd is now the folder paulrun was started from.
  • Blocks get PAULRUN_RUNBOOK_DIR, the folder the runbook is in, so a runbook can still use files kept next to it.
  • Running a runbook shows the folder blocks will run in, as directory: straight after the title, so you can check it before answering Start?. --dry shows it too.
  • paulrun library, the book picker and paulrun inputs are in colour in a terminal: names you type are bold cyan, details are dim, and secrets and problems stand out. Piped output has no colour, as before.
  • Inputs can have a default, shown at the prompt and used when you press enter. The environment still comes first. check reports a default that isn't text, doesn't match the input's pattern, or is on a secret.
  • Inputs can have choices: the only values accepted, listed at the prompt. You type the choice itself, and a value from the environment has to be one of them too. check reports choices that aren't a list of text, a choice the pattern refuses, a default that isn't a choice, and choices on a secret.

Initial release. paulrun runs hand-written markdown runbooks.

  • paulrun go runs a runbook's steps in order, streaming each block's output as it's printed and stopping at the first block that fails.
  • run blocks for shell (sh, bash, shell) and Python (python, py), with the python frontmatter key to choose the interpreter.
  • docstring blocks to show notes as the runbook runs, and confirm blocks to pause for steps done by hand.
  • input blocks to ask for a value part way through a run, once it exists: a pull request number from a step done by hand, or a one-time code that expires in seconds.
  • Inputs, collected from the environment or by asking, with an optional pattern to check them against. Plain inputs fill in <NAME> placeholders; secrets are hidden as you type them and replaced with **** everywhere paulrun shows or records them.
  • paulrun go --dry to see every block with its inputs filled in, without running anything.
  • paulrun go --step to run, skip or quit at each block.
  • Transcripts: with output_path set, every run is added to a plain record of what ran, what it printed and how it finished.
  • Ctrl-C stops a run cleanly, letting a running block stop and recording how far the run got.
  • paulrun check to find problems before running anything: missing or malformed frontmatter, undeclared placeholders, secrets used as placeholders, blocks outside a step, and shell and Python syntax errors, with shellcheck warnings when it's installed.
  • paulrun inputs to list the inputs a runbook needs, and paulrun backends to list the languages paulrun can run.
  • Backends for other languages can be added by any package, through the paulrun.backends entry point group.

docs.title: 🔌 Backends
docs.text:
A backend runs run blocks for one or more languages. paulrun comes with two, for shell and Python, and other languages can be added by any package.

Run paulrun backends to see which backends are installed, the languages each one runs, and the package it comes from:

python  python, py       paulrun.backends.python:PythonBackend (paulrun 0.2.0)
shell   sh, bash, shell  paulrun.backends.shell:ShellBackend (paulrun 0.2.0)

docs.title: Built-in backends
docs.text: Backend Languages Needs See shell sh, bash, shell bash Shell blocks python python, py nothing extra Python blocks

docs.title: Writing a backend
docs.text:
A backend is a plain class with a name, the languages it runs, and two methods: validate() checks a block, and run() runs it. It doesn't need a base class, only to match this protocol from paulrun.backends:

class Backend(Protocol):
    """Runs `run` blocks for one or more languages.

    Backends are classes registered under the `paulrun.backends` entry point group. Each is created
    once, with no arguments, when backends are loaded.
    """

    # Read-only, so a backend can set them as plain class attributes.
    @property
    def name(self) -> str: ...

    @property
    def languages(self) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        """The fence languages this backend runs, e.g. ("sh", "bash")."""

    def validate(self, code: str) -> list[Problem]:
        """Return the problems found in a block, without running it. An empty list means it's fine.

        code is the block as written, so it can contain <NAME> placeholders. Replacing them with
        something this language accepts is up to the backend. Any error stops the runbook running;
        warnings are only reported.
        """

    def run(
        self,
        code: str,
        *,
        frontmatter: Mapping[str, Any],
        env: Mapping[str, str],
        cwd: Path,
        output: Callable[[str], None],
    ) -> int:
        """Run a block and return its exit code, where 0 means it succeeded.

        Call output with each line the block prints, without its newline, as soon as it's printed.
        Don't print anything directly; paulrun owns the terminal. frontmatter is the runbook's
        frontmatter, read-only. env is the block's complete environment and cwd is where it runs.
        """

Everything a backend needs is in paulrun.backends (Problem, stream and Interrupted) and paulrun.inputs (PLACEHOLDER).

docs.title: validate()
docs.text:
paulrun check and paulrun run call validate() on every block before anything runs. It returns a list of Problems:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Problem:
    """Something a backend found wrong with a block."""

    message: str
    line: int | None = None  # line in the block, counting its first line as 1; None if it's about the whole block
    warning: bool = False  # warnings are reported but don't stop the runbook running
  • Lines count from the block's first line, as 1. paulrun turns them into lines in the runbook.
  • An error stops the run; a warning is only shown.

  • The code still has its <NAME> placeholders. Swap each for something your language accepts before checking it. The built-in backends use the bare name:

    from paulrun.inputs import PLACEHOLDER

script = PLACEHOLDER.sub(lambda match: match.group(1), code)

  • Check that what run() needs is installed, so a missing tool is reported before anything runs.

docs.title: run()
docs.text:
run() gets:

  • code: the block with its placeholders filled in. Secrets are only in env.
  • frontmatter: the runbook's frontmatter, read-only, for settings of your own.
  • env: the block's complete environment. Pass it on as it is.
  • cwd: where the block runs, the folder paulrun was started from.
  • output: call it with each line the block prints, as it's printed.

It returns the block's exit code. A backend never prints: paulrun shows each line, masks secrets and records the transcript.

docs.title: stream()
docs.text:
Most backends run a command, and stream() does all of that for you:

def stream(command: Sequence[str], *, env: Mapping[str, str], cwd: Path, output: Callable[[str], None]) -> int:

It runs command, passes each line to output as it's printed, and returns the exit code. The built-in backends use it, because it gets the details right:

  • stdout and stderr are merged, in the order they were printed.
  • The command shares paulrun's terminal, so it can still ask for a password.
  • Ctrl-C works. The first press lets the command stop by itself; a second kills it and everything it started. Then stream() raises Interrupted with the exit code.

A backend that doesn't use stream() should also raise Interrupted(exit_code) once its block has stopped after Ctrl-C.

docs.title: Shipping your own backend
docs.text:
Anyone can publish a backend in their own package, and once it's installed alongside paulrun, it loads like a built-in one. Here's a complete backend for Node.js, in a package called paulrun-node:

paulrun-node/
  pyproject.toml
  paulrun_node/
    __init__.py

paulrun_node/__init__.py:

import re
import shutil
import subprocess
from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from paulrun.backends import Problem, stream
from paulrun.inputs import PLACEHOLDER


class NodeBackend:
    """Runs each block as a Node.js script."""

    name = "node"
    languages = ("js", "javascript")

    def validate(self, code: str) -> list[Problem]:
        if shutil.which("node") is None:
            return [Problem("node isn't installed")]
        # Swap each placeholder for its bare name, which is a plain identifier, so the code still parses.
        script = PLACEHOLDER.sub(lambda match: match.group(1), code)
        result = subprocess.run(["node", "--check"], input=script, capture_output=True, text=True)
        if result.returncode == 0:
            return []
        # node starts with where the error is, e.g. "[stdin]:3", and says what it is further down.
        where = re.match(r"\[stdin\]:(\d+)", result.stderr)
        errors = [line for line in result.stderr.splitlines() if line.startswith("SyntaxError: ")]
        return [Problem(errors[0] if errors else result.stderr.strip(), line=int(where.group(1)) if where else None)]

    def run(
        self,
        code: str,
        *,
        frontmatter: Mapping[str, Any],
        env: Mapping[str, str],
        cwd: Path,
        output: Callable[[str], None],
    ) -> int:
        return stream(["node", "-e", code], env=env, cwd=cwd, output=output)

pyproject.toml registers it under the paulrun.backends entry point group:

[project]
name = "paulrun-node"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = ["paulrun>=0.1.0"]

[project.entry-points."paulrun.backends"]
node = "paulrun_node:NodeBackend"

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

Install it alongside paulrun:

uv tool install paulrun --with paulrun-node     # once it's on PyPI
uv tool install paulrun --with ./paulrun-node   # from a local folder, while you work on it

With pip, install it into paulrun's environment. Then paulrun backends lists it:

node    js, javascript   paulrun_node:NodeBackend (paulrun-node 0.1.0)
python  python, py       paulrun.backends.python:PythonBackend (paulrun 0.2.0)
shell   sh, bash, shell  paulrun.backends.shell:ShellBackend (paulrun 0.2.0)

and runbooks can use it:

---
title: Hello from Node
---

## Say hello

```js run
console.log(`Hello from Node ${process.version}`);
```

To test a backend, call its methods directly: run() with output=lines.append, then check the exit code and lines, and validate() on a broken block. See paulrun's backend tests.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Each language can only have one backend. If two claim the same language, paulrun stops with an error naming both.
  • Frontmatter keys of your own get a check warning, since check only knows paulrun's keys. It doesn't stop a run.

docs.title: Adding a backend to paulrun
docs.text:
A backend for a widely used language can ship with paulrun itself. It's the same code, in a different place:

  1. paulrun/backends/<name>.py, implementing the protocol. shell.py and python.py are good models.

  2. One entry point line in paulrun's pyproject.toml, next to the built-in ones:

    [project.entry-points."paulrun.backends"]
shell = "paulrun.backends.shell:ShellBackend"
python = "paulrun.backends.python:PythonBackend"

    Then run make install, and uv run paulrun backends should list it.

  3. tests/backends/test_<name>.py, which really runs blocks in tmp_path, skipped if the language isn't installed, e.g. pytest.mark.skipif(shutil.which("ruby") is None, reason="ruby isn't installed"). If GitHub's ubuntu-latest doesn't have the language, add a step to .github/workflows/ci.yml that installs it.

  4. A row in Built-in backends, and a section in the runbook format on how its blocks run.
  5. A CHANGELOG entry, in both CHANGELOG.md and docs/CHANGELOG.md.

CONTRIBUTING.md has the rest: setting up, and what to run before opening a pull request.

docs.title: 📟 Command line
docs.text:
paulrun RUNBOOK [--dry] [--step | --no-step]      # run a runbook
paulrun run RUNBOOK [--dry] [--step | --no-step]  # the same, in full
paulrun check RUNBOOK                             # find problems without running anything
paulrun inputs RUNBOOK                            # list the inputs a runbook needs
paulrun library                                   # list the books in your runbook library
paulrun backends                                  # list the languages paulrun can run
paulrun --version

paulrun on its own shows this list.

docs.title: Naming a runbook
docs.text:
RUNBOOK is a file, or the name of a book in your runbook library:

paulrun RELEASING.md        # the file RELEASING.md, here
paulrun rebuild-frontend    # the book rebuild-frontend.md, in your library
  1. If RUNBOOK is a file that exists, that's the runbook, so a file is never hidden by a book with the same name.
  2. Otherwise, if it has no /, it's the book <name>.md in your library. The .md is optional.
  3. Otherwise it's a usage error, which names both places paulrun looked:
Error: Invalid value for 'RUNBOOK': no runbook 'rebuild-frontend': no such file here, and no rebuild-frontend.md in the library at /home/you/runbooks

docs.title: paulrun run
docs.text:
Runs a runbook, step by step.

paulrun RELEASING.md

You don't need to type run: anything after paulrun that isn't a command is a runbook. Options go before or after it, so paulrun RELEASING.md --dry is the same as paulrun --dry RELEASING.md. Use paulrun run check to run a book called check.md, since paulrun check is the command.

  1. Checks the runbook, as paulrun check does. Errors stop it here.
  2. Collects the inputs. See Inputs.
  3. Shows the plan and asks Start? [y/N].
  4. Runs each step in order, streaming each block's output as it's printed.
VERSION (The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0): 1.2.0
Release my-package
directory: /home/you/Projects/my-package
inputs: VERSION=1.2.0
  1. Run the tests
  2. Tag the release
  3. Publish on GitHub
2 run blocks
Start? [y/N] y

=== Run the tests ===
    make test
...
exit 0 (4.2s)

=== Tag the release ===
    git tag 1.2.0
...
exit 0 (0.1s)

=== Publish on GitHub ===
Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0.
Continue? [y/N] y

finished: ok (12.8s)
transcript: logs/release-1.2.0.md

directory: is where blocks will run. See Where blocks run.

The run stops at the first block that fails:

=== Build ===
    echo "Building"
    exit 2
Building
exit 2 (0.0s)

finished: failed at "Build" (exit 2)

Only y answers Start? and Continue? with yes. Anything else, including enter, ends the run as aborted.

docs.title: Picking a book
docs.text:
With no runbook, paulrun run asks which book from your library to run:

$ paulrun run
  1. rebuild-frontend     Rebuild the frontend
  2. update-project-deps  Update a project's dependencies
Run which? (q to quit) 1

Answer with a number. --dry and --step work too. Answer q, or press enter, to stop without running anything.

docs.title: --dry
docs.text:
Shows what the runbook would do, without running anything.

paulrun --dry RELEASING.md
  • Every block is shown with its inputs filled in.
  • There's no Start?, confirm blocks don't wait, and no transcript is written.
  • Secrets and input blocks aren't asked for.
VERSION (The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0): 1.2.0
Release my-package
directory: /home/you/Projects/my-package
inputs: VERSION=1.2.0
  1. Run the tests
  2. Tag the release
  3. Publish on GitHub
2 run blocks
dry run: nothing will be run

=== Run the tests ===
    make test

=== Tag the release ===
    git tag 1.2.0

=== Publish on GitHub ===
Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0.

finished: dry run, nothing was run

docs.title: --step
docs.text:
Asks before running each run block.

paulrun --step RELEASING.md

=== Build ===
    echo "Building"
Run this block? [y]es / [s]kip / [q]uit y
Building
exit 0 (0.0s)

=== Publish ===
    echo "Publishing"
Run this block? [y]es / [s]kip / [q]uit s
skipped

finished: ok (0.0s)

y runs the block, s skips it, and q ends the run as aborted. With --dry, --step does nothing, since nothing runs.

A runbook that should always be run this way can set step: true in its frontmatter, so you don't need to remember --step. To run one of those straight through, pass --no-step.

docs.title: Pressing Ctrl-C
docs.text:
• A running block gets the Ctrl-C too, and paulrun waits for it to stop.
  • If a block ignores it, press Ctrl-C again to stop the block and everything it started.
  • The run ends as finished: interrupted at "<step>".

docs.title: paulrun check
docs.text:
Finds problems in a runbook without running anything.

paulrun check RELEASING.md

RELEASING.md: ok

Each problem is shown with its line, so your editor can jump to it:

broken.md:6: error: input VERSION is declared twice (first on line 4)
broken.md:8: warning: input BRANCH is never used
broken.md:12: error: run blocks must be inside a step (a ## heading)
broken.md:19: error: <TAG> isn't a declared input
broken.md:21: error: syntax error near unexpected token `fi'

4 errors, 1 warning

Errors stop the runbook running:

  • a missing title, or a frontmatter value of the wrong type
  • an input without a name or description, a name that isn't UPPER_SNAKE_CASE or is declared twice, or a pattern that isn't a valid regular expression
  • a default or choices that can't work. See Defaults and Choices.
  • a placeholder that isn't a declared input, or a secret used as a placeholder
  • an input block that isn't valid YAML, or is used before it's asked for
  • a block before the first ## heading
  • a run block in a language no backend runs, or a python command that isn't installed
  • a syntax error in a shell or Python block

Warnings don't:

  • a frontmatter or input key paulrun doesn't know, often a typo
  • an input nothing uses
  • a Python SyntaxWarning, and shellcheck findings if it's installed

docs.title: paulrun inputs
docs.text:
Lists the inputs a runbook needs, so you know what to have ready.

paulrun inputs PUBLISHING.md

VERSION  The version being released, e.g. 1.2.0
         pattern: ^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$
BRANCH   The branch to release from
         default: main
PR       The number GitHub gave the pull request
         pattern: ^\d+$
         asked in "Open the pull request"
OTP      The code from your authenticator app
         pattern: ^\d{6}$
         secret
         asked in "Publish"

Inputs from input blocks come last, with the step that asks for them. Frontmatter inputs are listed even if the rest of the runbook is broken.

docs.title: paulrun library
docs.text:
Lists the books in your runbook library, with each one's title and description.

$ paulrun library
library: /home/you/runbooks
rebuild-frontend     Rebuild the frontend
                     Clean install the frontend's dependencies, then rebuild it.
update-project-deps  Update a project's dependencies

A book whose frontmatter can't be read is still listed, with why.

docs.title: paulrun backends
docs.text:
Lists the languages paulrun can run, and the package each comes from.

$ paulrun backends
python  python, py       paulrun.backends.python:PythonBackend (paulrun 0.2.0)
shell   sh, bash, shell  paulrun.backends.shell:ShellBackend (paulrun 0.2.0)

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 The run finished, or check found no errors. 1 A block failed, the run was aborted or interrupted, check found errors, or the runbook couldn't be read. 2 The command was used wrongly, e.g. a runbook that doesn't exist.

docs.title: 🚀 Install
docs.text: paulrun is a command-line tool, so install it on its own rather than into a project:

docs.title: uv
docs.text: uv tool install paulrun

docs.title: pip
docs.text:
pip install paulrun

Once installed, check it's working:

> paulrun --version
paulrun, version 0.2.0

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or later.
  • macOS or Linux. Windows isn't supported.
  • bash, which runs shell blocks. It's on macOS and almost every Linux system already.

docs.title: Optional: shellcheck
docs.text:
If shellcheck is installed, paulrun check uses it to warn about common mistakes in shell blocks, such as an unquoted variable. Without it, shell blocks are still checked for syntax errors.

brew install shellcheck      # macOS
sudo apt install shellcheck  # Debian and Ubuntu

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• The runbook format to write your first runbook
  • The command line to see everything paulrun can do

docs.title: 📚 Your runbook library
docs.text:
Some runbooks belong to a project, like the RELEASING.md at the root of a package. Others are jobs you do the same way across every project. Those go in your runbook library.

Your library is a directory of markdown files that paulrun can execute, and we call these books. Move a book there once, and run it by name from wherever you are:

cd ~/Projects/website
paulrun rebuild-frontend

docs.title: Where your library is
docs.text:
Your library is ~/runbooks. Every .md file directly inside it is a book, named after its file: ~/runbooks/rebuild-frontend.md is the book rebuild-frontend. Folders and other files in it aren't books, so ~/runbooks/logs/ is a fine place for transcripts.

To keep it somewhere else, set PAULRUN_LIBRARY:

export PAULRUN_LIBRARY=~/work-runbooks

docs.title: Running a book
docs.text:
paulrun rebuild-frontend        # run it
paulrun --dry rebuild-frontend  # see what it would do first
paulrun check rebuild-frontend  # find problems in it

A file in the current directory always comes first, so a book never hides a runbook in your project. See Naming a runbook.

A book runs in the directory you're in, not in your library, and paulrun shows it as directory: before anything runs. See Where blocks run.

docs.title: Finding a book
docs.text:
paulrun library lists your books, with each one's title and description:

$ paulrun library
library: /home/you/runbooks
rebuild-frontend     Rebuild the frontend
                     Clean install the frontend's dependencies under nvm, then rebuild it.
update-project-deps  Update a project's dependencies

Or run paulrun run with no runbook, and pick one by number:

$ paulrun run
  1. rebuild-frontend     Rebuild the frontend
  2. update-project-deps  Update a project's dependencies
Run which? (q to quit) 1

docs.title: Example: rebuilding a frontend under nvm
docs.text:
This book clean-installs a frontend's dependencies with the Node version the project asks for, then rebuilds it. Save it as ~/runbooks/rebuild-frontend.md, and run it from the project's root.

---
title: Rebuild the frontend
description: Clean install the frontend's dependencies under nvm, then rebuild it.
inputs:
  - name: FE_SET
    description: Which frontend set to rebuild
    choices: [main, admin, all]
    default: main
---

# Rebuild the frontend

Run this from the project's root. It uses the Node version in
`frontend/.nvmrc`, and needs [nvm](https://github.com/nvm-sh/nvm).

## Check the project

```sh run
test -f frontend/.nvmrc || { echo "No frontend/.nvmrc here; run this from the project's root."; exit 1; }
```

## Clean install and rebuild

nvm is a shell function your profile loads, so the block loads it itself.
Everything that needs the project's Node is in this one block, since a later
block would be back on your default Node.

```sh run
source "$NVM_DIR/nvm.sh"
cd frontend
nvm install
nvm use
rm -rf node_modules
npm ci
npm run build -- --set=<FE_SET>
```

Two things in it apply to any book:

  • Load what your profile sets up. paulrun runs shell blocks with a plain bash, which doesn't read your profile, so shell functions like nvm, pyenv and rbenv aren't there. source them in the block.
  • Keep one environment in one block. A cd or nvm use is gone by the next block, and that fails quietly: the next block just runs with your default Node. So everything that needs the project's Node goes in the block with nvm use.

docs.title: 📜 Runbook format
docs.text:
A runbook is a markdown file. Frontmatter at the top sets it up, each ## heading is a step, and code blocks marked for paulrun are shown, paused on, or run. Everything else is documentation.

Run paulrun check on a runbook to find anything wrong with it.

docs.title: Frontmatter
docs.text:
YAML between --- lines at the top of the file:

---
title: Release my-package                    # required
description: Release a new version.          # optional
output_path: logs/release-<VERSION>.md       # optional
python: uv run python                        # optional
step: true                                   # optional, default false
inputs:                                      # optional
  - name: VERSION                            # required
    description: The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0   # required
    pattern: '^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$'               # optional
  - name: PUBLISH_TOKEN
    description: Token for the package index
    secret: true                             # optional, default false
---
Key What it does title The runbook's name, shown when it runs. Required. description What it's for, shown by paulrun library. output_path Where to keep a transcript of each run. python The command that runs Python blocks. step true to ask before each run block, as --step does, without having to pass it. --no-step turns it off for one run. inputs Values to ask for. See Inputs.

Any other key is a check warning, so a typo like ouput_path gets noticed.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Values a runbook needs each time it runs, such as the version being released.

Key What it does name Required, in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, e.g. VERSION. description Required. Shown when paulrun asks for it. pattern A regular expression the whole value must match, e.g. '^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$'. secret true for passwords and tokens. See Secrets. default Used if you press enter. See Defaults. choices The only values accepted. See Choices.

paulrun collects every input before the first step:

  1. If an environment variable with the input's name is set, it's used: VERSION=1.2.0 paulrun RELEASING.md doesn't ask. An empty variable counts as not set.
  2. Otherwise paulrun asks for it.

A typed answer that doesn't fit the input's pattern or choices is asked for again. A value from the environment that doesn't fit stops paulrun before anything runs.

docs.title: Using inputs
docs.text:
Every input is an environment variable in every run block: $VERSION in shell, os.environ["VERSION"] in Python.

An input that isn't secret can also be written as a placeholder, <VERSION>, in run, docstring and confirm blocks and in output_path. paulrun fills it in. The rest of the runbook is never changed.

A placeholder that isn't a declared input is a check error, and an input nothing uses, as <VERSION> or $VERSION, is a warning.

Placeholders are filled in as plain text

If someone enters 1.2.0; rm -rf ~ for <VERSION>, that's what the block runs. Give inputs used in commands a pattern.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
inputs:
  - name: BRANCH
    description: The branch to release from
    default: main

BRANCH (The branch to release from) [main]:

Pressing enter takes main. The environment still comes first, and a default must still match the input's pattern.

Quote a default YAML would read as something other than text, such as default: '1.10', which would otherwise be the number 1.1. A secret can't have a default.

docs.title: Choices
docs.text:
inputs:
  - name: FE_SET
    description: Which frontend set to rebuild
    choices: [comms, billing, all]
    default: comms

FE_SET (Which frontend set to rebuild) [comms] (comms, billing, all): everything
FE_SET must be one of: comms, billing, all

Type the choice itself, not its number. Choices are compared exactly, so Comms isn't comms. A default must be one of the choices, every choice must match the pattern if there is one, and a secret can't have choices.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
An input with secret: true is never shown or saved:

  • Its prompt hides what's typed.
  • It's never a placeholder. Read it as $PUBLISH_TOKEN; writing <PUBLISH_TOKEN> is a check error.
  • Its value is shown as **** in block output and the transcript.
  • paulrun --dry doesn't ask for it.
uv publish --token "$PUBLISH_TOKEN"

Note

paulrun spots a secret by its exact value, one line at a time. A command that encodes it, or splits it across lines, can still reveal it. Pass secrets to commands rather than printing them.

docs.title: Input blocks
docs.text:
Some values only exist part way through a run, like the number GitHub gives a pull request you've just opened. An input block asks for one when the run reaches it:

## Open the pull request

```confirm
Open a pull request for <VERSION> on GitHub.
```

```input
name: PR
description: The number GitHub gave the pull request
pattern: '^\d+$'
```

```sh run
gh pr merge <PR>
```

It takes the same keys as a frontmatter input, and works the same from then on.

  • Using it before the block, or in output_path, is a check error.
  • paulrun --dry doesn't ask for it, and shows <PR> as written.

A one-time code is a good use of a secret input block:

```input
name: OTP
description: The code from your authenticator app
pattern: '^\d{6}$'
secret: true
```

```sh run
npm publish --otp "$OTP"
```

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Each ## heading starts a step, named by its text. ### and smaller headings are just text inside the step.

A block before the first ## heading is a check error.

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text:
The first word of a code block's opening line is its language. A second word of run makes paulrun run it.

Block What paulrun does ```docstring Shows the text. ```confirm Shows the text and waits for y. Any other answer ends the run. ```input Asks for an input. See Input blocks. ```sh run Runs it. See Run blocks. Anything else, e.g. ```sh Nothing. It's documentation.

So a plain ```sh block shows a command without paulrun running it.

```docstring
Releasing <VERSION>. This takes a few minutes.
```

```confirm
Create a GitHub release from tag <VERSION>, then come back here.
```

docs.title: Run blocks
docs.text:
paulrun shows each block's output as it's printed. Exit code 0 carries on; anything else stops the run.

Every block runs with paulrun's environment and every input, plus:

  • PAULRUN_RUNBOOK_DIR, the folder the runbook is in
  • PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, so Python output isn't held back
  • PAGER=cat and GIT_PAGER=cat, so nothing waits in a pager

Run paulrun backends to see which languages you can use, or add your own with backends.

docs.title: Where blocks run
docs.text:
Blocks run in the folder you run paulrun from, not the runbook's folder. So one runbook can work on whichever project you're in:

cd ~/Projects/website
paulrun ~/runbooks/update-deps.md

Use $PAULRUN_RUNBOOK_DIR for files kept next to the runbook:

cp "$PAULRUN_RUNBOOK_DIR/templates/pull-request.md" .github/

Each block is its own process, so a cd or export is gone by the next block. Keep commands that need them together.

docs.title: Shell blocks
docs.text: sh, bash or shell. Each block is one bash script that stops at the first failing command, as if it began with set -eo pipefail. check finds syntax errors, and shellcheck warnings if it's installed.

docs.title: Python blocks
docs.text:
python or py. Each block is its own script, run with the Python paulrun runs on, so only the standard library is available. To use another interpreter or your project's dependencies, set python:

python: uv run python

check compiles each block with paulrun's own Python, so syntax only a newer Python understands isn't caught.

docs.title: Blocks that ask questions
docs.text: A block can still ask on the terminal, the way git and ssh ask for a password. But output is shown a line at a time, so a question with no newline after it isn't shown until you answer. Use inputs for values instead.

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
Set output_path, and each run is added to the end of that file, so a failed attempt and the rerun that fixed it are both kept:

output_path: logs/release-<VERSION>.md

A relative path is relative to the folder you run paulrun from. Missing folders are created, and --dry runs aren't recorded.

--- paulrun RELEASING.md @ 2026-10-12T15:11:27+01:00
--- inputs: VERSION=1.2.0 PUBLISH_TOKEN=****

=== Run the tests ===
    make test
<everything make test printed>
exit 0 (4.2s)

=== Publish on GitHub ===
confirm: Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0. -> yes

=== Publish to PyPI ===
input: OTP=****
    uv publish --token "$PUBLISH_TOKEN"
skipped

--- finished: ok (3m12s)

The last line says how the run ended:

Last line When --- finished: ok (3m12s) Every step ran. --- finished: failed at "<step>" (exit N) A block exited with N. --- finished: aborted at "<step>" A confirm wasn't answered y, or you quit with --step. --- finished: interrupted at "<step>" You pressed Ctrl-C.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• bash on macOS is version 3.2, which can't spot an unclosed heredoc (cat <<EOF with no EOF).
  • Windows isn't supported.
